sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Chapter purpose: guidance on construction QA/QC inspection for micropiles. Inspection ensures construction follows plans and specifications. The responsible party for QA/QC depends on the contracting approach: method spec (owner QA and QC), performance spec (contractor QC, owner limited QA), and design-build (contractor QA with owner random checks or independent third party). Short-term and long-term performance monitoring is usually conducted by the owner agency.
sections.body: The purpose of this chapter is to provide guidance regarding construction monitoring and inspection (QA/QC) for micropiles. Inspection is the primary mechanism to assure that micropiles are constructed in accordance with project plans and specifications. Short-term and long-term monitoring may be conducted to assess the performance of the micropiles. Construction monitoring activities can be carried out by the owner agency, the contractor, or both, depending on the contracting approach. Under the method contracting approach, both QA and QC activities are typically carried out by the owner agency. Under the performance contracting approach, the contractor carries out QC activities and the owner agency carries out a limited number of QA activities to verify that material, equipment, construction tolerance, and sequencing requirements are met. Under the design-build approach, all required QA inspection activities are carried out by the contractor or are the contractor's responsibility in accordance with an approved QA plan. Random QA tests are done by the owner agency or independent third-party inspection firm.
key_points: Inspection ensures construction compliance with plans and specifications
Method spec: owner agency performs both QA and QC
Performance spec: contractor does QC; owner does limited QA for materials, tolerances, sequencing
Design-build: contractor responsible for QA per approved QA plan; owner does random checks or uses independent firm
Long-term performance monitoring usually conducted by owner agency
sections.applicability: Construction quality assurance and quality control for all micropile project types.

sections.title: Inspection Roles Under Certain Contract Approaches
sections.summary: Describes the division of QA and QC responsibilities under method, performance, and design-build contracting approaches. Under method specifications, the owner's inspector is the primary QA agent and must verify strict compliance. Under performance specifications, the contractor takes primary responsibility for QC while the owner verifies key acceptance requirements. Under design-build, the contractor manages QA with owner review of the QA plan and periodic independent verification.
sections.body: The owner's inspector performs construction monitoring to verify compliance with the contract documents and provide quality assurance. The owner's inspection is conducted to assure strict compliance with each component of the specification. Under the performance contracting approach, the contractor carries out QC activities. The owner agency will carry out a limited number of QA activities as required by project specifications, primarily to verify that requirements are met for materials, equipment, construction tolerances, and sequencing. The contractor selects the equipment and construction procedures used and is responsible for satisfying specified performance criteria. For the design-build approach, the performance of all required QA inspection activities is carried out by the contractor or is the responsibility of the contractor in accordance with the QA plan approved by the owner. Random QA tests are performed by the owner agency or through an independent third-party inspection firm.
key_points: Owner's inspector: verify strict compliance with contract documents under method specifications
Performance spec: contractor selects equipment and procedures; responsible for meeting performance criteria
Design-build: contractor develops and implements QA plan, approved by owner
Owner reserves right to random QA testing under performance and design-build approaches
Independent third-party inspectors may be used under design-build approach
sections.applicability: Clarifying QA/QC responsibilities before project begins under each contracting approach.

sections.title: Pre-Project Preparation
sections.summary: Prior to construction, the QA inspector must review a 15-item pre-construction submittal from the contractor. Items include: capacity requirements per pile, drilling equipment (manufacturer, model, flushing media), installation plan (sequence, phasing, scheduling), grout mix design (batching, mixing, injection), reinforcement details, post-grouting methods, utility protection plan, and load testing plan. The inspector uses this to understand the planned work and identify potential deviations during construction.
sections.body: Prior to construction, the QA inspector must review the contractor's pre-construction submittals. These submittals should at minimum include: (1) installer qualifications demonstrating experience with similar projects; (2) project overview and schedule; (3) drawings and specifications review; (4) micropile layout plan; (5) geotechnical information; (6) capacity requirements for each micropile; (7) drilling equipment including manufacturer, model numbers, flushing media, and precautions to minimize drilling deviations; (8) list of all equipment to be used with equipment loads on structure or adjacent ground during construction; (9) general installation plan including proposed sequence, phasing, and scheduling; (10) grout design mix with batching, mixing, and injection techniques; (11) reinforcement sizing, configuration, and corrosion protection; (12) post-grouting methods (if anticipated), procedure, and equipment; (13) documentation of and protection methods for existing utilities and sensitive elements; (14) plan to accommodate low headroom or nearby obstructions; and (15) load testing information including identification of test locations, equipment, and procedures.
key_points: 15-item pre-construction submittal required before work begins
Inspector reviews: capacity requirements, drilling equipment, grout mix, reinforcement, post-grouting
Contractor must document utility protection plan and sensitivity of adjacent structures
Load testing plan (locations, equipment, procedures) must be reviewed before testing begins
Installation sequence and scheduling reviewed to identify phasing risks

sections.applicability: Pre-construction checklist for QA inspector review before micropile installation begins.

sections.title: Inspection of Micropile Materials
sections.summary: All micropile materials must be inspected upon delivery and prior to installation. Compliance is verified by: (1) manufacturer/supplier certification; (2) visual inspection and product literature review; or (3) conformance testing. Cement: verify type, storage conditions (Figure 8-2), and protection from hydration. Reinforcing steel: lift with fiber ropes, require mill certificates, verify corrosion condition (light rust acceptable; deep pitting = rejection). Mill secondary pipe requires tensile/chemical testing. Epoxy-coated and double-corrosion-protected bars need special handling.
sections.body: Specifications describe minimum requirements for micropile materials. These requirements may be defined explicitly or by reference to standard specifications such as those from AASHTO and ASTM. Conformance to specification requirements is commonly assessed by: (1) reviewing manufacturer or supplier certification submitted by the contractor; (2) reviewing product literature and visual inspection; or (3) conformance testing. All materials and prefabricated elements delivered to the site must be visually examined prior to installation. Cement storage should protect against moisture and contamination. Steel reinforcement should be stored above the ground surface and protected against mechanical damage and weather exposure. Reinforcing bars should be lifted using fiber ropes or webbing and supported at several points to prevent excessive bending. Mill certificates should accompany all reinforcing steel. Mill secondary pipe materials (for which mill certificates are not available) require verification of steel quality through tensile and chemical testing of samples. For Buy America Contracts, United States manufacturing of materials must be verified. Visual inspection should check for corrosion: a light coating of surface rust is normal and acceptable; deep flaky corrosion or pitting is cause for rejection. Epoxy-coated bars and double corrosion-protected bars require special handling: padded bands and padded supports; repairs to epoxy coatings per manufacturer recommendations.
key_points: Three compliance verification approaches: certification, visual inspection, or conformance testing
All materials must be visually examined before installation
Reinforcing steel: fiber rope lifting, mill certificates required, verify bar size
Mill secondary pipe: no mill certificate available — requires tensile and chemical testing
Light surface rust acceptable; deep flaky corrosion or pitting = rejection
Epoxy-coated bars: padded bands and supports; repair epoxy damage per manufacturer
Buy America: verify US manufacturing for applicable contracts
figures: Figure 8-4: Double Corrosion Protected (Encapsulated) Reinforcing Steel
sections.applicability: Receiving inspection for all micropile materials: cement, steel casing, reinforcing bars, and specialty corrosion-protection systems.

sections.title: Inspection of Construction Activities
sections.summary: Construction inspection covers drilling, reinforcement placement, and grouting. Drilling: monitor for unacceptable loss of ground (signs: inability to withdraw casing, excessive soil removal, surface subsidence). Reinforcement: verify centralizer spacing at 2.5-3m intervals, ensure centering. Grouting: verify grout mix, inject via tremie from bottom up, maintain positive grout head, limit pressure grouting to prevent ground distress (2-4 MPa typical for post-grouting). All operations should proceed continuously to avoid hole deterioration.
sections.body: Inspection of Drilling Activities: The contractor's drilling operation should not cause unacceptable loss of ground. Signs of unacceptable loss of ground include: inability to withdraw the drill casing from the hole; large quantity of soil removal with little or no casing advancement; and subsidence of the ground above the drilling location. When temporary casing is to be removed during grouting, it should be removed without disturbing or damaging pile reinforcement. The casing should be kept full of grout during removal to minimize drillhole collapse. Drilling, reinforcement installation, and grouting of each micropile should be completed in a series of continuous processes. For consolidating clays and weak rock, the entire process should be completed in one day. Temporarily plug or cover drillholes between operations. Maintain casing at least 0.3m (1 ft) above ground surface to keep hole clean. Inspection of Reinforcement Placement: Centralizers and spacers should be placed at specified intervals, typically 2.5 to 3m. Verify attachment to reinforcement (tie-wire or duct tape) and that reinforcement remains centered in the borehole. Inspection of Grouting Activities: Verify grout mix design before grouting begins. Inject via tremie tube from the bottom of the hole until grout of equal quality returns at the top. Maintain a positive head at the grout holding tank to avoid drawing air into the grout. Post-grouting injection pressures typically 2-4 MPa (290-580 psi); documented pressures have exceeded 6.5 MPa (943 psi). Maintain detailed grouting records (see Section 8.6.3).
key_points: Loss of ground signs: casing sticking, excessive soil removal, surface subsidence
Remove temporary casing while maintaining grout fill to prevent hole collapse
Complete drilling, reinforcement, and grouting as continuous processes same day for weak/sensitive materials
Maintain casing >= 0.3m above grade to prevent contamination of completed holes
Centralizers at 2.5-3m intervals; verify centering of reinforcement
Tremie grouting from bottom up; maintain positive grout head in tank
Post-grouting pressures: typically 2-4 MPa; documented up to 6.5 MPa
sections.applicability: Field inspection of micropile drilling, reinforcement placement, and grouting operations.

sections.title: Required Project Documentation
sections.summary: Three documentation requirements: (1) Load test records including test pile installation method, equipment, and load-displacement data. (2) Production micropile installation log (Tables 8-1/8-2) for each pile: design vs. as-built dimensions, drill method, soil descriptions, flush return, grouting data. (3) Grouting records: daily grout production and consumption, pressure and volume per pile, specific gravity checks (Baroid Mud Balance per API RP 13B-1; target SG=1.8-1.9, w/c≈0.45), and 3 grout cube compressive strength tests per AASHTO T106/ASTM C-109.
sections.body: Three types of project documentation are required. Load Testing Documentation: During micropile load testing, the inspector must verify that: (1) the test pile installation method used is the same as will be used for production piles; (2) load testing equipment and reference frames are properly set up; and (3) all load-displacement data are accurately recorded. Production Micropile Installation Log: Comprehensive records of the installation are required for payment basis and identification of significant deviations. Table 8-1 provides a standard installation log template; Table 8-2 shows a completed example. Log entries include: pile designation number, design vs. as-built dimensions (inclination, casing diameter/wall thickness, reinforcement, casing length, bond length, total pile length), installation dates and times, drill method, drill rig, drill bit type and size, depth-by-depth soil/rock descriptions, flush return descriptions, and grouting data. Grouting Records: Grout production and consumption records must be kept daily. The actual pressure and volume of grout pumped for each micropile must be recorded. Grout quality is assessed by: unconfined compressive strength per AASHTO T106/ASTM C-109 using three 50-mm (2 in.) grout cubes per set; and specific gravity (density) per API RP 13B-1 Baroid Mud Balance Test. A common specific gravity for grout is between 1.8 and 1.9, corresponding to a water/cement ratio of approximately 0.45. Density testing should be performed at least once per micropile since it is quick and inexpensive and allows immediate reaction to anomalies.
key_points: Production log (Table 8-1): record design vs. as-built for every pile — dimensions, drill method, soil descriptions, grout data
Grouting records required daily: pressure and volume per pile
Grout strength: 3 cubes (50mm) per AASHTO T106/ASTM C-109; results after 48 hours
Grout density: Baroid Mud Balance per API RP 13B-1; perform at least once per pile
Target grout SG = 1.8-1.9 corresponds to w/c ≈ 0.45
Density test preferred as immediate quality check vs. strength test (48-hour lag)
